entries.a2079e96876787bff73ecf00aba5b046bb5f0fdd: <div sID="gen20476" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Mic.6" sID="Mic.6"/> <div eID="gen20476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20478" type="x-p"/> After the precious promises in the two foregoing chapters, relating to the Messiah's kingdom, the prophet is here directed to set the sins of Israel in order before them, for their conviction and humiliation, as necessary to make way for the comfort of gospel-grace. Christ's forerunner was a reprover, and preached repentance, and so prepared his way. Here, I. God enters an action against his people for their base ingratitude, and the bad returns they had made him for his favours, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.1-Mic.6.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He shows the wrong course they should have taken, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. He calls upon them to hear the voice of his judgments, and sets the sins in order before them for which he still proceeded in his controversy with them (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.9">ver. 9</reference>), their injustice (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.16">ver. 16</reference>), for both which ruin was coming upon them.
entries.68cb2672716c027d6cbf2cc6cf896e05718aa6f3: <div eID="gen20478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20477" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Expostulations with His People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear ye now what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saith; Arise, contend thou before the mountains, and let the hills hear thy voice. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear ye, O mountains, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel. <hi type="super">3</hi> O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me. <hi type="super">4</hi> For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. <hi type="super">5</hi> O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20480" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prefaces to the message are very solemn and such as may engage our most serious attention. 1. The people are commanded to give audience: <hi type="italic">Hear you now what the Lord says.</hi> What the prophet speaks he speaks from God, and in his name; they are therefore bound to hear it, not as the word of a sinful dying man, but of the holy living God. <hi type="italic">Hear now</hi> what he saith, for, first or last, he will be heard. 2. The prophet is commanded to speak in earnest, and to put an emphasis upon what he said: <hi type="italic">Arise, contend thou before the mountains,</hi> or <hi type="italic">with the mountains,</hi> and <hi type="italic">let the hills hear thy voice,</hi> if it were possible; contend with the mountains and hills of Judea, that is, with the inhabitants of those mountains and hills; and, some think, reference is had to those mountains and hills on which they worshipped idols and which were thus polluted. But it is rather to be taken more generally, as appears by his call, not only to the mountains, but to the <hi type="italic">strong foundations of the earth,</hi> pursuant to the instructions given him. This is designed, (1.) To excite the earnestness of the prophet; he must speak as vehemently as if he designed to make even the hills and mountains hear him, must <hi type="italic">cry aloud, and not spare;</hi> what he had to say in God's name he must proclaim publicly before the mountains, as one that was neither ashamed nor afraid to own his message; he must speak as one concerned, as one that desired to speak to the heart, and therefore appeared to speak from the heart. (2.) To expose the stupidity of the people; "<hi type="italic">Let the hills hear thy voice,</hi> for this senseless careless people will not hear it, will not heed it. Let the rocks, the <hi type="italic">foundations of the earth,</hi> that have no ears, hear, since Israel, that has ears, will not hear." It is an appeal to the mountains and hills; let them bear witness that Israel has fair warning given them, and good counsel, if they would but take it. Thus Isaiah begins with, <hi type="italic">Hear, O heavens! and give ear, O earth!</hi> Let them <hi type="italic">judge between God and his vineyard.</hi> <div eID="gen20480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20481" type="x-p"/> II. The message itself is very affecting. He is to let all the world know that God has a quarrel with his people, good ground for an action against them. Their offences are public, and therefore so are the articles of impeachment exhibited against them. Take notice <hi type="italic">the Lord has a controversy with his people and he will plead with Israel,</hi> will plead by his prophets, plead by his providences, to make good his charge. Note, 1. Sin begets a controversy between God and man. The righteous God has an action against every sinner, an action of debt, an action of trespass, an action of slander. 2. If Israel, God's own professing people, provoke him by sin, he will let them know that he has a controversy with them; he sees sin in them, and is displeased with it, nay, their sins are more displeasing to him than the sins of others, as they are a greater grief to his Spirit and dishonour to his name. 3. God will plead with those whom he has a controversy with, will plead with his people Israel, that they may be convinced and that he may be justified. In the close of the foregoing chapter he pleaded with the heathen in anger and fury, to bring them to ruin; but here he pleads with Israel in compassion and tenderness, to bring them to repentance, <hi type="italic">Come now, and let us reason together.</hi> God reasons with us, to teach us to reason with ourselves. See the equity of God's cause, it will bear to be pleaded, and sinners themselves will be forced to confess judgment, and to own that <hi type="italic">God's ways are equal,</hi> but their <hi type="italic">ways are unequal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.25">Ezek. xviii. 25</reference>. Now, (1.) God here challenges them to show what he had done against them which might give them occasion to desert him. They had revolted from God and rebelled against him; but had they any cause to do so? (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O my people! what have I done unto thee? Wherein have I wearied thee?</hi>" If subjects quit their allegiance to their prince, they will pretend (as the ten tribes did when they revolted from Rehoboam), that his yoke is too heavy for them; but can you pretend any such thing? <hi type="italic">What have I done to you</hi> that is unjust or unkind? <hi type="italic">Wherein have I wearied you</hi> with the impositions of service or the exactions of tribute? <hi type="italic">Have I made you to serve with an offering?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.23">Isa. xliii. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">What iniquity have your fathers found in me?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.5">Jer. ii. 5</reference>. He never deceived us, nor disappointed our expectations from him, never did us wrong, nor put disgrace upon us; why then do we wrong and dishonour him, and frustrate his expectations from us? Here is a challenge to all that ever were in God's service to testify against him if they have found him, in any thing, a hard Master, or if they have found his demands unreasonable. (2.) Since they could not show any thing that he had done against them, he will show them a great deal that he has done for them, which should have engaged them for ever to his service, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.4-Mic.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. They are here directed, and we in them, to look a great way back in their reviews of the divine favour; let them remember their former days, their first days, when they were formed into a people, and the great things God did for them, [1.] When he brought them out of Egypt, the land of their bondage, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.4">v. 4</reference>. They were content with their slavery, and almost in love with their chains, for the sake of the garlic and onions they had plenty of; but God <hi type="italic">brought them up,</hi> inspired them with an ambition of liberty and animated them with a resolution by a bold effort to shake off their fetters. The Egyptians held them fast, and would not let the people go; but God <hi type="italic">redeemed them,</hi> not by price, but by force, <hi type="italic">out of the house of servants,</hi> or, rather, <hi type="italic">the house of bondage,</hi> for it is the same word that is used in the preface to the ten commandments, which insinuates that the considerations which are arguments for duty, if they be not improved by us, will be improved against us as aggravations of sin. When he brought them out of Egypt into a vast howling wilderness, as he left not himself without witness, so he left not them without guides, for he sent before them <hi type="italic">Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, three prophets</hi> (says the Chaldee paraphrase), Moses the great prophet of the Old Testament, Aaron his prophet (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exod. vii. 1</reference>), and Miriam a prophetess, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exod. xv. 20</reference>. Note, When we are calling to mind God's former mercies to us we must not forget the mercy of good teachers and governors when we were young; let those be made mention of, to the glory of God, who went before us, saying, <hi type="italic">This is the way, walk in it;</hi> it was God that sent them before us, to prepare the way of the Lord and to prepare a people for him. [2.] When he brought them into Canaan. God no less glorified himself, and honoured them, in what he did for them when he brought them into the land of their rest than in what he did for them when he brought them out of the land of their servitude. When Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, were dead, yet they found God the same. Let them remember now what God did for them, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In baffling and defeating the designs of Balak and Balaam against them, which he did by the power he has over the hearts and tongues of men, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.5">v. 5</reference>. Let them remember <hi type="italic">what Balak the king of Moab consulted,</hi> what mischief he devised and designed to do to Israel, when they encamped in the plains of Moab; that which he consulted was to <hi type="italic">curse Israel,</hi> to divide between them and their God, and to disengage him from the protection of them. Among the heathen, when they made war upon any people, they endeavoured by magic charms or otherwise to get from them their tutelar gods, as to rob Troy of its Palladium. Macrobius has a chapter <hi type="italic">de ritu evocandi Deos—concerning the solemnity of calling out the gods.</hi> Balak would try this against Israel; but remember <hi type="italic">what Balaam the son of Beor answered him,</hi> how contrary to his own intention and inclination; instead of cursing Israel, he blessed them, to the extreme confusion and vexation of Balak. Let them remember the malice of the heathen against them, and for that reason never <hi type="italic">learn the way of the heathen,</hi> nor associate with them. Let them remember the kindness of their God to them, how he <hi type="italic">turned the curse into a blessing (because the Lord thy God loved thee,</hi> as it is, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.5">Deut. xxiii. 5</reference>), and for that reason never forsake him. Note, The disappointing of the devices of the church's enemies ought always to be remembered to the glory of the church's protector, who can make <hi type="italic">the answer of the tongue</hi> directly to contradict the preparation and consultation of the heart, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Prov. xvi. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In bringing them <hi type="italic">from Shittim,</hi> their last lodgment out of Canaan, <hi type="italic">unto Gilgal,</hi> their first lodgment in Canaan. There it was, between Shittim and Gilgal, that, upon the death of Moses, Joshua, a type of Christ, was raised up to put Israel in possession of the land of promise and to fight their battles; there it was that they passed over Jordan through the divided waters, and renewed the covenant of circumcision; these mercies of God to their fathers they must now remember, that they may <hi type="italic">know the righteousness of the Lord, his righteousness</hi> (so the word is), his justice in destroying the Canaanites, his goodness in giving rest to his people Israel, and his faithfulness to his promise made unto the fathers. The remembrance of what God had done to them might convince them of all this, and engage them for ever to his service. Or they may refer to the controversy now pleaded between God and Israel; let them remember God's many favours to them and their fathers, and compare with them their unworthy ungrateful conduct towards him, <hi type="italic">that they may know the righteousness of the Lord</hi> in contending with them, and it may appear that in this controversy he has right on his side; his ways are equal, for he will be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks,</hi> and <hi type="italic">clear when he judges.</hi>
entries.59cf9e870bb1e73fd613d766a7895a72ac512a1a: <div eID="gen20481" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Anxiety Respecting the Divine Favour. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20482" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Wherewith shall I come before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and</hi> bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? <hi type="super">7</hi> Will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be pleased with thousands of rams, <hi type="italic">or</hi> with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn <hi type="italic">for</hi> my transgression, the fruit of my body <hi type="italic">for</hi> the sin of my soul? <hi type="super">8</hi> He hath shewed thee, O man, what <hi type="italic">is</hi> good; and what doth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God? <div eID="gen20482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20483" type="x-p"/> Here is the proposal for accommodation between God and Israel, the parties that were at variance in the beginning of the chapter. Upon the trial, judgment is given against Israel; they are convicted of injustice and ingratitude towards God, the crimes with which they stood charged. Their guilt is too plain to be denied, too great to be excused, and therefore, <div eID="gen20483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20484" type="x-p"/> I. They express their desires to be at peace with God upon any terms (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherewith shall I come before the Lord?</hi> Being made sensible of the justice of God's controversy with them, and dreading the consequences of it, they were inquisitive what they might do to be reconciled to God and to make him their friend. They apply to a proper person, with this enquiry, to the prophet, the Lord's messenger, by whose ministry they had been convinced. Who so fit to show them their way as he that had made them sensible of their having missed it? And it is observable that each one speaks for himself: <hi type="italic">Wherewith shall I come?</hi> Knowing every one the plague of his own heart, they ask, not, <hi type="italic">What shall this man do?</hi> But, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> Note, Deep convictions of guilt and wrath will put men upon careful enquiries after peace and pardon, and then, and not till then, there begins to be some hope of them. They enquire <hi type="italic">wherewith they may come before the Lord, and bow themselves before the high God.</hi> They believe there is a God, that he is Jehovah, and that he is the <hi type="italic">high God,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Most High.</hi> Those whose consciences are convinced learn to speak very honourably of God, whom before they spoke slightly of. Now, 1. We know we must <hi type="italic">come before God;</hi> he is the God with whom <hi type="italic">we have to do;</hi> we must come as subjects, to pay our homage to him, as beggars, to ask alms from him, nay, we must <hi type="italic">come before him,</hi> as criminals, to receive our doom from him, must come before him as our Judge. 2. When we come before him we must <hi type="italic">bow before him;</hi> it is our duty to be very humble and reverent in our approaches to him; and, when we come before him, there is no remedy but we must submit; it is to no purpose to contend with him. 3. When we come and bow before him it is our great concern to find favour with him, and to be accepted of him; their enquiry is, <hi type="italic">What will the Lord be pleased with?</hi> Note, All that rightly understand their own interest cannot but be solicitous what they must do to please God, to avoid his displeasure and to obtain his good-will. 4. In order to God's being pleased with us, our care must be that the sin by which we have displeased him may be taken away, and an atonement made for it. The enquiry here is, <hi type="italic">What shall I give for my transgression,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the sin of my soul?</hi> Note, The transgression we are guilty of is the sin of our soul, for the soul acts it (without the soul's act it is not sin) and the soul suffers by it; it is the disorder, disease, and defilement of the soul, and threatens to be the death of it: <hi type="italic">What shall I give for my transgressions?</hi> What will be accepted as a satisfaction to his justice, a reparation of his honour? And what will avail to shelter me from his wrath? 5. We must therefore ask, <hi type="italic">Wherewith may we come before him?</hi> We must not appear before the Lord empty. What shall we bring with us? In what manner must we come? In whose name must we come? We have not that in ourselves which will recommend us to him, but must have it from another. What righteousness then shall we appear before him in? <div eID="gen20484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20485" type="x-p"/> II. They make proposals, such as they are, in order to it. Their enquiry was very good and right, and what we are all concerned to make, but their proposals betray their ignorance, though they show their zeal; let us examine them:— <div eID="gen20485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20486" type="x-p"/> 1. They bid high. They offer, (1.) That which is very rich and costly—<hi type="italic">thousands of rams.</hi> God required one ram for a sin-offering; they proffer flocks of them, their whole stock, will be content to make themselves beggars, so that they may but be at peace with God. They will bring the best they have, the rams, and the most of them, till it comes to thousands. (2.) That which is very dear to them, and which they would be most loth to part with. They could be content to part with <hi type="italic">their first-born for their transgressions,</hi> if that would be accepted as an atonement, and the <hi type="italic">fruit of their body for the sin of their soul.</hi> To those that had become <hi type="italic">vain in their imaginations</hi> this seemed a probable expedient of making satisfaction for sin, because our children are pieces of ourselves; and therefore the heathen sacrificed their children, to appease their offended deities. Note, Those that are thoroughly convinced of sin, of the malignity of it, and of their misery and danger by reason of it, would give all the world, if they had it, for peace and pardon. <div eID="gen20486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20487" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet they do not bid right. It is true some of these things were instituted by the ceremonial law, as the bringing of burnt-offerings to God's altar, and calves of a year old, rams for sin-offerings, and oil for the meat-offerings; but these alone would not recommend them to God. God had often declared that <hi type="italic">to obey is better than sacrifice,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">hearken than the fat of rams,</hi> that <hi type="italic">sacrifice</hi> and <hi type="italic">offering he would not;</hi> the legal sacrifices had their virtue and value from the institution, and the reference they had to Christ the great propitiation; but otherwise, of themselves, it was <hi type="italic">impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sin.</hi> And as to the other things here mentioned, (1.) Some of them are impracticable things, as <hi type="italic">rivers of oil,</hi> which nature has not provided to feed men's luxury, but rivers of water to supply men's necessity. All the proposals of peace but those that are according to the gospel are absurd. One stream of the blood of Christ is worth ten thousand rivers of oil. (2.) Some of them are wicked things, as to give our <hi type="italic">first-born</hi> and the <hi type="italic">fruit of our body</hi> to death, which would but add to the transgression and the <hi type="italic">sin of the soul.</hi> He that hates robbery for burnt-offerings much more hates murder, such murder. What right have we to our <hi type="italic">first born</hi> and the <hi type="italic">fruit of our body?</hi> Do they not belong to God? Are they not his already, and born to him? Are they not sinners by nature, and their lives forfeited upon their own account? How then can they be a ransom for ours? (3.) They are all external things, parts of that bodily exercise which profiteth little, and which could not <hi type="italic">make the comers thereunto perfect.</hi> (4.) They are all insignificant, and insufficient to attain the end proposed; they could not answer the demands of divine justice, nor satisfy the wrong done to God in his honour by sin, nor would they serve in lieu of the sanctification of the heart and the reformation of the life. Men will part with any thing rather than their sins, but they part with nothing to God's acceptance unless they part with them. <div eID="gen20487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20488" type="x-p"/> III. God tells them plainly what he demands, and insists upon, from those that would be accepted of him, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Let their money perish with them that think the pardon of sin and the favour of God may be so purchased; no, <hi type="italic">God has shown thee, O man! what is good.</hi> Here we are told, <div eID="gen20488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20489" type="x-p"/> 1. That God has made a discovery of his mind and will to us, for the rectifying of our mistakes and the direction of our practice. (1.) It is God himself that has shown us what we must do. We need not trouble ourselves to make proposals, the terms are already settled and laid down. He whom we have offended, and to whom we are accountable, has told us upon what conditions he will be reconciled to us. (2.) It is to man that he has shown it, not only to thee, <hi type="italic">O Israel!</hi> but <hi type="italic">to thee, O man!</hi> Gentiles as well as Jews—to men, who are rational creatures, and capable of receiving the discovery, and not to brutes,—to men, for whom a remedy is provided, not to devils, whose case is desperate. What is spoken to <hi type="italic">all men every where</hi> in general, must by faith be applied to ourselves in particular, as if it were spoken <hi type="italic">to thee, O man!</hi> by name, and to no other. (3.) It is a discovery of <hi type="italic">that which is good,</hi> and which <hi type="italic">the Lord requires of us.</hi> He has shown us our end, which we should aim at, in showing us what is good, wherein our true happiness does consist; he has shown us our way in which we must walk towards that end in showing us what he requires of us. There is something which God requires we should do for him and devote to him; and it is good. It is good in itself; there is an innate goodness in moral duties, antecedent to the command; they are not, as ceremonial observances, good because they are commanded, but commanded because they are good, consonant to the eternal rule and reason of good and evil, which are unalterable. It has likewise a direct tendency to our good; our conformity to it is not only the condition of our future happiness, but is a great expedient of our present happiness; <hi type="italic">in keeping</hi> God's <hi type="italic">commandments there is great reward,</hi> as well as after keeping them. (4.) It is shown us. God has not only made it known, but made it plain; he has discovered it to us with such convincing evidence as amounts to a demonstration. <hi type="italic">Lo this, we have searched it, so it is.</hi> <div eID="gen20489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20490" type="x-p"/> 2. What that discovery is. The good which God requires of us is not the paying of a price for the pardon of sin and acceptance with God, but doing the duty which is the condition of our interest in the pardon purchased. (1.) We must <hi type="italic">do justly,</hi> must <hi type="italic">render to all their due,</hi> according as our relation and obligation to them are; we must do wrong to none, but do right to all, in their bodies, goods, and good name. (2.) We must <hi type="italic">love mercy;</hi> we must delight in it, as our God does, must be glad of an opportunity to do good, and do it cheerfully. Justice is put before mercy, for we must not give that in alms which is wrongfully got, or with which our debts should be paid. <hi type="italic">God hates robbery for a burnt-offering.</hi> (3.) We must <hi type="italic">walk humbly with our God.</hi> This includes all the duties of the first table, as the two former include all the duties of the second table. We must take the Lord for our God in covenant, must attend on him and adhere to him as ours, and must make it our constant care and business to please him. Enoch's walking with God is interpreted (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.5">Heb. xi. 5</reference>) his <hi type="italic">pleasing God.</hi> We must, in the whole course of our conversation, conform ourselves to the will of God, keep up our communion with God, and study to approve ourselves to him in our integrity; and this we must do humbly (submitting our understandings to the truths of God and our will to his precepts and providences); we must <hi type="italic">humble ourselves to walk with God</hi> (so the margin reads it); every thought within us must be brought down, to be brought into obedience to God, if we would walk comfortably with him. This is that which God requires, and without which the most costly services are <hi type="italic">vain oblations;</hi> this is more than <hi type="italic">all burnt-offerings and sacrifices.</hi>
entries.1d7121ab451fb58299ecbd28a3f50a32d7b77f72: <div eID="gen20490" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Accusations and Threatenings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20491" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's voice crieth unto the city, and <hi type="italic">the man of</hi> wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it. <hi type="super">10</hi> Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure <hi type="italic">that is</hi> abominable? <hi type="super">11</hi> Shall I count <hi type="italic">them</hi> pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights? <hi type="super">12</hi> For the rich men thereof are full of violence, and the inhabitants thereof have spoken lies, and their tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> deceitful in their mouth. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore also will I make <hi type="italic">thee</hi> sick in smiting thee, in making <hi type="italic">thee</hi> desolate because of thy sins. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied; and thy casting down <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in the midst of thee; and thou shalt take hold, but shalt not deliver; and <hi type="italic">that</hi> which thou deliverest will I give up to the sword. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap; thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine. <hi type="super">16</hi> For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof a hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people. <div eID="gen20491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20492" type="x-p"/> God, having shown them how necessary it was that they should do justly, here shows them how plain it was that they had done unjustly; and since they submitted not to his controversy, nor went the right way to have it taken up, here he proceeds in it. Observe, <div eID="gen20492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20493" type="x-p"/> I. How the action is entered against them, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.9">v. 9</reference>. God speaks to <hi type="italic">the city,</hi> to Jerusalem, to Samaria. His <hi type="italic">voice cries</hi> to it by his servants the prophets who were to <hi type="italic">cry aloud and not spare.</hi> Note, The voice of the prophets is <hi type="italic">the Lord's voice,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">cries to the city,</hi> cries to the country. <hi type="italic">Doth not wisdom cry?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.1">Prov. viii. 1</reference>. When the sin of a city cries to God his voice cries against the city; and, when the judgments of God are coming upon a city, his voice first <hi type="italic">cries unto it.</hi> He warns before he wounds, because he is <hi type="italic">not willing that any should perish.</hi> Now observe, 1. How the voice of God is discerned by some: <hi type="italic">The man of wisdom will see thy name.</hi> When the voice of God cries to us we may by it see his name, may discern and perceive that by which he makes himself known. Yet many see it not, are not aware of it, because they do not regard it. God <hi type="italic">speaks once, yea, twice, and they perceive it not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job xxxiii. 14</reference>); but those that are men of wisdom will see it, and perceive it, and make a good use of it. Note, It is a point of true wisdom to discover the name of God in the voice of God, and to learn what he is from what he says. <hi type="italic">Wisdom shall see thy name,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the knowledge of the holy is understanding.</hi> 2. What this voice of God says to all: "<hi type="italic">Hear you the rod, and who hath appointed it.</hi> Hear the rod when it is coming; hear it at a distance, before you see it and feel it; and be awakened to go forth to meet the Lord in the way of his judgments. Hear the rod when it has come, and is actually upon you, and you are sensible of the smart of it; hear what it says to you, what convictions, what counsels, what cautions, it speaks to you." Note, Every rod has a voice, and it is the voice of God that is to be heard in the rod of God, and it is well for those that understand the language of it, which if we would do we must have an eye to <hi type="italic">him that appointed it.</hi> Note, Every rod is appointed, of what kind it shall be, where it shall light, and how long it shall lie. God in every affliction <hi type="italic">performs the thing that is appointed for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job xxiii. 14</reference>), and to him therefore we must have an eye, to him we must have an ear; we must hear what he says to us by the affliction. <hi type="italic">Hear it, and know it for thy good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.6">Job v. 6</reference>. The work of ministers is to explain the providences of God and to quicken and direct men to learn the lessons that are taught by them. <div eID="gen20493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20494" type="x-p"/> II. What is the ground of the action, and what are the things that are laid to their charge. <div eID="gen20494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20495" type="x-p"/> 1. They are charged with injustice, a sin against the second table. Are there yet to be found among them the marks and means of fraudulent dealing? What! after all the methods that God has taken to teach them to do justly, will they yet deal unjustly? It seems, they will, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.10">v. 10</reference>. And <hi type="italic">shall I count them pure?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.6.11">v. 11</reference>. No; this is a sin which will by no means consist with a profession of purity. Those that are dishonest in their dealings have not the spots of God's children, and shall never be reckoned pure, whatever shows of devotion they may make. <hi type="italic">Be not deceived, God is not mocked.</hi> When a man is suspected of theft, or fraud, the justice of peace will send a warrant to search his house. God here does, as it were, search the houses of those citizens, and there he finds, (1.) <hi type="italic">Treasures of wickedness,</hi> abundance of wealth, but it is ill-got, and not likely to prosper; for <hi type="italic">treasures of wickedness profit nothing.</hi> (2.) A <hi type="italic">scant measure,</hi> by which they sold to the poor, and so exacted upon them and cheated them. (3.) They had <hi type="italic">wicked balances and a bag of false weights,</hi> by which, under a pretence of weighing what they sold, and giving the buyer what was right, they did him the greatest wrong, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.11">v. 11</reference>. (4.) Those that had wealth and power in their hands abused it to oppression and extortion; <hi type="italic">The rich men thereof are full of violence;</hi> for those that have much would have more, and are in a capacity of making it more by the power which their abundance of wealth gives them. They are <hi type="italic">full of violence,</hi> that is, they have their houses full of that which is got by violence. (5.) Those that had not the advantage of doing wrong by their wealth yet found means of defrauding those they dealt with: <hi type="italic">The inhabitants thereof have spoken lies;</hi> if they are not able to use force and violence, they use fraud and deceit; the <hi type="italic">inhabitants</hi> have <hi type="italic">spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth;</hi> they do not stick at a deliberate lie, to make a good bargain. Some understand it of their speaking falsely concerning God, saying, <hi type="italic">The Lord seeth not; he hath forsaken the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Ezek. viii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen20495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20496" type="x-p"/> 2. They are charged with idolatry (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The statutes of Omri are kept, and all the work of the house of Ahab.</hi> Both these kings were wicked, and <hi type="italic">did evil in the sight of the Lord;</hi> but the wickedness which they established by a law, concerning which they made statutes, and which was the peculiar work of that house, was idolatry. Omri walked in the way of Jeroboam, and <hi type="italic">in his sin of provoking God to anger with their vanities,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.26">1 Kings xvi. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">31</reference>. Ahab introduced the worship of Baal. These reigns were some ages before the time when this prophet lived, and yet the wickedness which they established by their laws and examples remained to this day; those statutes were still kept, and that work was still done; and the princes and people still <hi type="italic">walked in their counsels,</hi> took the same measures, and governed themselves and the people by the same politics. Observe, (1.) The same wickedness continued from one generation to another. Sin is a <hi type="italic">root of bitterness,</hi> soon planted, but not so soon plucked up again. The iniquity of former ages is often transmitted to, and entailed upon, the succeeding ones. Those that make corrupt laws, and bring in corrupt usages, are doing that which perhaps may prove the ruin of the child unborn. (2.) It was not the less evil in itself, provoking to God, and dangerous to the sinners, for its having been established and confirmed by the laws of princes, the examples of great men, and a long prescription. Though the worship of idols is enacted by the statutes of Omri, recommended by the practice of the house of Ahab, and pleads that it has been the usage of many generations, yet it is still displeasing to God and destructive to Israel; for no laws nor customs are of force against the divine command. <div eID="gen20496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20497" type="x-p"/> III. What is the judgment given upon this. Being found guilty of these crimes, the sentence is that that which God had given them warning of (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.9">v. 9</reference>) shall be brought upon them (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore also will I make thee sick, in smiting thee.</hi> As they had smitten the poor with the rod of their oppressions, so would God in like manner smite them, so as to make them sick, sick of the gains they had unjustly gotten, so that though they had <hi type="italic">swallowed down riches</hi> they should <hi type="italic">vomit them up again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.15">Job xx. 15</reference>. Their doom is, <div eID="gen20497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20498" type="x-p"/> 1. That what they have they shall not have any comfortable enjoyment of; it shall do them no good. They grasped at more than enough, but, when they have it, it shall not be enough to make them easy and happy. What is got by fraud and oppression cannot be kept or enjoyed with any satisfaction. (1.) Their food shall not nourish them: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied,</hi> either because the food shall not digest, for want of God's blessing going along with it, or because the appetite shall by disease be made insatiable and still craving, the just punishment of those that were greedy of gain and enlarged their desires as hell. Men may be surfeited with the good things of this world and yet not satisfied, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Eccl. v. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. (2.) Their country shall not harbour and protect them: "<hi type="italic">Thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee,</hi> that is, thou shalt be broken and ruined by the intestine troubles, mischiefs at home enough to cast thee down, though thou shouldst not be invaded by a foreign force." God can cast a nation down by that which is in the midst of them, can consume them by a fire in their own bowels. (3.) They shall not be able to preserve what they have from a foreign force, nor to recover what they have lost: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt take hold</hi> of what is about to be taken from thee, but thou shalt not hold it fast, shalt catch at it, but <hi type="italic">shalt not deliver it,</hi> shalt not retrieve it." It is meant of their wives and children, that were very dear to them, which they took hold of, as resolved not to part with them, but there is no remedy, they must go into captivity. Note, What we hold closest we commonly lose soonest, and that proves least safe which is most dear. (4.) What they save for a time shall be reserved for a future and sorer stroke: <hi type="italic">That which thou deliverest</hi> out of the hand of one enemy <hi type="italic">will I give up to the sword</hi> of another enemy; for God has many arrows in his quiver; if one miss the sinner, the next shall not. (5.) What they have laboured for they shall not enjoy (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap;</hi> it shall be blasted and withered, and there shall be nothing to reap, or an enemy shall come and reap it for himself, or thou shalt be carried into captivity, and leave it to be reaped by thou knowest not whom. Thou shalt <hi type="italic">tread the olives,</hi> but <hi type="italic">thou shalt not anoint thyself with oil,</hi> having no heart to make use of ornaments and refreshments when all is going to ruin. Thou shalt tread out <hi type="italic">the sweet wine,</hi> but <hi type="italic">shalt not drink wine,</hi> for many things may fall between the cup and the lip." Note, It is very grievous to be disappointed of our expectations, and not to have the pleasure of that which we have taken pains for; and this will be the just punishment of those that frustrate God's expectations from them, and answer not the cost he has been at upon them. See this threatened in the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev. xxvi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30 Deut.28.38">Deut. xxviii. 30, 38</reference>, &c.; and compare <reference osisRef="Isa.62.8-Isa.62.9">Isa. lxii. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen20498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20499" type="x-p"/> 2. That all they have shall at length be taken from them (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be made desolate because of thy sins;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Mic.6.16">v. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">a desolation and a hissing.</hi> Sin makes a nation desolate; and when a people that have been famous and flourishing are made desolate it is the astonishment of some and the triumph of others; some lament it, and others hiss at it. Thus <hi type="italic">you shall bear the reproach of my people.</hi> Their being the people of God, in name and profession while they kept close to their duty and kept themselves in his love, was an honour to them, and all their neighbours thought it so; but now that they have corrupted and ruined themselves, now that their sins and God's judgments have made their land desolate, their having been once the people of God does but turn so much the more to their reproach; their enemies will say, <hi type="italic">These are the people of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.20">Ezek. xxxvi. 20</reference>. Note, If professors of religion ruin themselves, their ruin will be the most reproachful of any; and they in a special manner will rise at the last day to everlasting shame and contempt.  <chapter eID="Mic.6"/> <div eID="gen20499" type="x-p"/>

entries.9b7582b50865b34d077f8727ab6cc78e2431eae0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12783"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.6.1-Mic.6.16">Mi 6:1-16</reference>. Appeal before All Creation to the Israelites to Testify, if They Can, if Jehovah Ever Did Aught but Acts of Kindness to Them from the Earliest Period: God Requires of Them Not So Much Sacrifices, as Real Piety and Justice: Their Impieties and Coming Punishment.</title> <div sID="gen23720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12783"/><hi type="bold">1. contend thou--</hi>Israel is called by Jehovah to plead with Him in controversy. <reference osisRef="Mic.5.11-Mic.5.13">Mi 5:11-13</reference> suggested the transition from those happy times described in the fourth and fifth chapters, to the prophet's own degenerate times and people.<div eID="gen23720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the mountains--</hi>in their presence; personified as if witnesses (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.1.2">Mi 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">De 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>). Not as the Margin, "with"; as God's controversy is with Israel, not with them. <div eID="gen23721" type="x-p"/>
entries.54e3f1700edd214b829f293e5d3a4217da3216a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12784"/><div sID="gen23722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12784"/><hi type="bold">2. Lord's controversy--</hi>How great is Jehovah's condescension, who, though the supreme Lord of all, yet wishes to prove to worms of the earth the equity of His dealings (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">Is 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">43:26</reference>). <div eID="gen23722" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1b8b9525f05238b6886dea3444eafe3068a4e55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12785"/><div sID="gen23723" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12785"/><hi type="bold">3. my people--</hi>the greatest aggravation of their sin, that God always treated them, and still treats them, as His people.<div eID="gen23723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what have I done unto thee?--</hi>save kindness, that thou revoltest from Me (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.5">Jr 2:5</reference>, 31).<div eID="gen23724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein have I wearied thee?--</hi>What commandments have I enjoined that should have wearied thee as irksome (<reference osisRef="1John.5.3">1Jo 5:3</reference>)? <div eID="gen23725" type="x-p"/>
entries.e40a28d60d0d8ea8ccf54c4477d4d677264402f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12786"/><div sID="gen23726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12786"/><hi type="bold">4. For--</hi>On the contrary, so far from doing anything harsh, I did thee every kindness from the earliest years of thy nationality.<div eID="gen23726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Miriam--</hi>mentioned, as being the prophetess who led the female chorus who sang the song of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Ex 15:20</reference>). God sent Moses to give the best laws; Aaron to pray for the people; Miriam as an example to the women of Israel. <div eID="gen23727" type="x-p"/>
entries.15c095460ccd24052385921fd4a037eca5459fb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12787"/><div sID="gen23728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12787"/><hi type="bold">5. what Balak ... consulted--</hi>how Balak plotted to destroy thee by getting Balaam to curse thee (<reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Nu 22:5</reference>).<div eID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what Balaam ... answered--</hi>how the avaricious prophet was constrained against his own will, to bless Israel whom he had desired to curse for the sake of Balak's reward (<reference osisRef="Num.24.9-Num.24.11">Nu 24:9-11</reference>) [Maurer]. Grotius explains it, "how Balaam answered, that the only way to injure thee was by tempting thee to idolatry and whoredom" (<reference osisRef="Num.31.16">Nu 31:16</reference>). The mention of "Shittim" agrees with this: as it was the scene of Israel's sin (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.5">Nu 25:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2Pe 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Re 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Shittim unto Gilgal--</hi>not that Balaam accompanied Israel from Shittim to Gilgal: for he was slain in Midian (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Nu 31:8</reference>). But the clause, "from Shittim," alone applies to Balaam. "Remember" God's kindnesses "from Shittim," the scene of Balaam's wicked counsel taking effect in Israel's sin, whereby Israel merited utter destruction but for God's sparing mercy, "to Gilgal," the place of Israel's first encampment in the promised land between Jericho and Jordan, where God renewed the covenant with Israel by circumcision (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.2-Josh.5.11">Jos 5:2-11</reference>).<div eID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know the righteousness--</hi>Recognize that, so far from God having treated thee harshly (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mi 6:3</reference>), His dealings have been kindness itself (so "righteous acts" for gracious, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.11">Jud 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">112:9</reference>). <div eID="gen23731" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f0d8c0fb414d18807d43849d1559cc236256010: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12788"/><div sID="gen23732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12788"/><hi type="bold">6. Wherewith shall I come before the Lord?--</hi>The people, convicted by the previous appeal of Jehovah to them, ask as if they knew not (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mi 6:8</reference>) what Jehovah requires of them to appease Him, adding that they are ready to offer an immense heap of sacrifices, and those the most costly, even to the fruit of their own body.<div eID="gen23732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burnt offerings--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.1.1-Lev.1.17">Le 1:1-17</reference>).<div eID="gen23733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calves of a year old--</hi>which used to be offered for a priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.2">Le 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen23734" type="x-p"/>
entries.d727be8c0f5190e34aab17f41c916e834147fed4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12789"/><div sID="gen23735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12789"/><hi type="bold">7. rivers of oil--</hi>used in sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Le 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>). Will God be appeased by my offering so much oil that it shall flow in myriads of torrents?<div eID="gen23735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my first-born--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.27">2Ki 3:27</reference>). As the king of Moab did.<div eID="gen23736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit of my body--</hi>my children, as an atonement (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.11">Psa 132:11</reference>). The Jews offered human sacrifices in the valley of Hinnom (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jr 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">32:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.27">Eze 23:27</reference>). <div eID="gen23737" type="x-p"/>
entries.c85946db992446b95208058e63aac961158bb7f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12790"/><div sID="gen23738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12790"/><hi type="bold">8. He--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath showed thee--</hi>long ago, so that thou needest not ask the question as if thou hadst never heard (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mi 6:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">De 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.11-Deut.30.14">30:11-14</reference>).<div eID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what is good--</hi>"the good things to come" under Messiah, of which "the law had the shadow." The Mosaic sacrifices were but suggestive foreshadowings of His better sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">He 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">10:1</reference>). To have this "good" first "showed," or revealed by the Spirit, is the only basis for the superstructure of the moral requirements which follow. Thus the way was prepared for the Gospel. The banishment of the Jews from Palestine is designed to preclude the possibility of their looking to the Mosaic rites for redemption, and shuts them up to Messiah.<div eID="gen23740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justly ... mercy--</hi>preferred by God to sacrifices. For the latter being positive ordinances, are only means designed with a view to the former, which being moral duties are the ends, and of everlasting obligation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.6">12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Am 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.24">24</reference>). Two duties towards man are specified--justice, or strict equity; and mercy, or a kindly abatement of what we might justly demand, and a hearty desire to do good to others.<div eID="gen23741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to walk humbly with thy God--</hi>passive and active obedience towards God. The three moral duties here are summed up by our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mt 23:23</reference>), "judgment, mercy, and faith" (in <reference osisRef="Luke.11.42">Lu 11:42</reference>, "the love of God"). Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jas 1:27</reference>. To walk with God implies constant prayer and watchfulness, familiar yet "humble" converse with God (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Ge 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">17:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23742" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f9418116ed1d12f9320672cb46848e3b9280fb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12791"/><div sID="gen23743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12791"/><hi type="bold">9. unto the city--</hi>Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man of wisdom--</hi>As in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.6">Pr 13:6</reference>, Hebrew, "sin" is used for "a man of sin," and in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, "prayer" for "a man of prayer"; so here "wisdom" for "the man of wisdom."<div eID="gen23744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall see thy name--</hi>shall regard Thee, in Thy revelations of Thyself. Compare the end of <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>. God's "name" expresses the sum-total of His revealed attributes. Contrast with this <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Is 26:10</reference>, "will not behold the majesty of the Lord." Another reading is adopted by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate, "there is deliverance for those who fear Thy name." English Version is better suited to the connection; and the rarity of the Hebrew expression, as compared with the frequency of that in the other reading, makes it less likely to be an interpolation.<div eID="gen23745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hear ... the rod, &c.--</hi>Hear what punishment (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mi 6:13</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">24</reference>) awaits you, and from whom. I am but a man, and so ye may disregard me; but remember my message is not mine, but God's. Hear the rod when it is come, and you feel its smart. Hear what counsels, what cautions it speaks.<div eID="gen23746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.47.7">Jr 47:7</reference>). <div eID="gen23747" type="x-p"/>

Are there yet--</hi>notwithstanding all My warnings. Is there to be no end of acquiring treasures by wickedness? Jehovah is speaking (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.9">Mi 6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scant measure ... abominable--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pr 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Am 8:5</reference>). <div eID="gen23749" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e69e71c21fcd6a71376ef8c6bb4ac1c5067b570: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12793"/><div sID="gen23750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12793"/><hi type="bold">11. Shall I count them pure--</hi>literally, "Shall I be pure with?" &c. With the pure God shows Himself pure; but with the froward God shows Himself froward (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>). Men often are changeable in their judgments. But God, in the case of the impure who use "wicked balances," cannot be pure, that is, cannot deal with them as He would with the pure. Vatablus and Henderson make the "I" to be "any one"; "Can I (that is, one) be innocent with wicked balances?" But as "I," in <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mi 6:13</reference>, refers to Jehovah, it must refer to Him also here.<div eID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bag--</hi>in which weights used to be carried, as well as money (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.13">De 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pr 16:11</reference>). <div eID="gen23751" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>rather, "Inasmuch as"; the conclusion "therefore," &c. following in <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mi 6:13</reference>.<div eID="gen23752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereof--</hi>of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen23753" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d227cca1c83ea06359efa35ea8dc1a600f94d58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12795"/><div sID="gen23754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12795"/><hi type="bold">13. make thee sick in smiting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Le 26:16</reference>, to which perhaps the allusion here is, as in <reference osisRef="Mic.6.14">Mi 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.17">Psa 107:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">Jr 13:13</reference>). <div eID="gen23754" type="x-p"/>
entries.97610110c1d11ef7f81c0844f94e3343d58a3982: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12796"/><div sID="gen23755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12796"/><hi type="bold">14. eat ... not be satisfied--</hi>fulfiling the threat, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">Le 26:26</reference>.<div eID="gen23755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee--</hi>Thou shalt be cast down, not merely on My borders, but in the midst of thee, thy metropolis and temple being overthrown [Tirinus]. Even though there should be no enemy, yet thou shalt be consumed with intestine evils [Calvin]. Maurer translates as from an Arabic root, "there shall be emptiness in thy belly." Similarly Grotius, "there shall be a sinking of thy belly (once filled with food), through hunger." This suits the parallelism to the first clause. But English Version maintains the parallelism sufficiently. The casting down in the midst of the land, including the failure of food, through the invasion thus answering to, "Thou shalt eat, and not be satisfied."<div eID="gen23756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt take hold, but ... not deliver--</hi>Thou shalt take hold (with thine arms), in order to save [Calvin] thy wives, children and goods. Maurer, from a different root, translates, "thou shalt remove them," in order to save them from the foe. But thou shalt fail in the attempt to deliver them (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jr 50:37</reference>).<div eID="gen23757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which thou deliverest--</hi>If haply thou dost rescue aught, it will be for a time: I will give it up to the foe's sword. <div eID="gen23758" type="x-p"/>
entries.633f2398ce847f3165a40a76f5469fdb585107ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12797"/><div sID="gen23759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12797"/><hi type="bold">15. sow ... not reap--</hi>fulfilling the threat (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Le 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.38-Deut.28.40">De 28:38-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Am 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen23759" type="x-p"/>
entries.577926ea9595014a52c77cc3cf06719eea1dd4e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12798"/><div sID="gen23760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12798"/><hi type="bold">16. statutes of Omri--</hi>the founder of Samaria and of Ahab's wicked house; and a supporter of Jeroboam's superstitions (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.16-1Kgs.16.28">1Ki 16:16-28</reference>). This verse is a recapitulation of what was more fully stated before, Judah's sin and consequent punishment. Judah, though at variance with Israel on all things else, imitated her impiety.<div eID="gen23760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">works of ... Ahab--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.25">1Ki 21:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen23761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye walk in their counsels--</hi>Though these superstitions were the fruit of their king's "counsels" as a master stroke of state policy, yet these pretexts were no excuse for setting at naught the counsels and will of God.<div eID="gen23762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I should make thee a desolation--</hi>Thy conduct is framed so, as if it was thy set purpose "that I should make thee a desolation."<div eID="gen23763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inhabitants thereof--</hi>namely, of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hissing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">La 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the reproach of my people--</hi>The very thing ye boast of, namely, that ye are "My people," will only increase the severity of your punishment. The greater My grace to you, the greater shall be your punishment for having despised it, Your being God's people in name, while walking in His love, was an honor; but now the name, without the reality, is only a "reproach" to you. <chapter eID="Mic.6"/>

entries.97e2a5f088e373fb3a5f8f176b7ef4bb3288312b: <div eID="gen34845" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34846" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34847" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34847" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34846" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34848" type="x-p"/> This chapter reproves and threatens. The manner of raising the attention by calling on man to urge his plea in the face of all nature, and on the inanimate creation to hear the expostulation of Jehovah with his people, is awakening and sublime. The words of Jehovah follow, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3-Mic.6.5">Mic 6:3-5</reference>. And God's mercies hawing been set forth to his people, one of them is introduced, in a beautiful dramatic form, asking what his duty is towards a God so gracious, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mic 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mic 6:7</reference>. The answer follows in the words of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mic 6:8</reference>; who goes on to upbraid the people of his charge with their injustice and idolatry, to which he ascribes want of success in their lawful undertakings, and those heave calamities which are now impending, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.9-Mic.6.15">Mic 6:9-15</reference>. <div eID="gen34848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34849" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34850" type="x-p"/> Arise, contend thou - This chapter is a sort of dialogue between God and the people. God speaks the five first verses, and convicts the people of sin, righteousness, and judgment. The People, convinced of their iniquity, deprecate God's judgments, in the sixth and seventh verses. In the eighth verse God prescribes the way in which they are to be saved; and then the prophet, by the command of God, goes on to remonstrate from the ninth verse to the end of the chapter.
entries.dce0cf9774fcd4f3081564b86e99f13e07856c7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34851" type="x-p"/> Hear ye, O mountains - Micah, as God's advocate, summons this people into judgment, and makes an appeal to inanimate creation against them. He had spoken to the priests, to the princes, to the people. He had done every thing that was necessary to make them wise, and holy, and happy; they had uniformly disobeyed, and were ever ungrateful. It was not consistent with either the justice or mercy of God to permit them to go on without reprehension and punishment. He now calls them into judgment; and such was the nature of their crimes that, to heighten the effect, and show what reason he had to punish such a people, he appeals to inanimate creation. Their ingratitude and rebellion are sufficient to make the mountains, the hills, and the strong foundations of the earth to hear, tremble, and give judgment against them. This, then, is the Lord's controversy with his people, and thus he will plead with Israel.
entries.78512c5031ebf66645d1722f06b6259a8b7bc256: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34852" type="x-p"/> O my people, what have I done unto thee? - They are called to show why God should not pronounce sentence upon them. This condescension is truly astonishing! God appears to humble himself to his creatures. You have acted basely, treacherously, and ungratefully to me; this had already been proved by the prophets. What cause have I given you for such conduct? I have required a religious service from you; but have I wearied you by a fatiguing round of difficult duties? If I have, now testify against me; and you shall be first heard, and your plea received, if it be reasonable and good. They are silent; and God proceeds, and states what he has done for them.
entries.660b2df3a78e7cc1380ffba37b233f678529dc32: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34853" type="x-p"/> I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt - Where you were slaves, and grievously oppressed; from all this I redeemed you. Was this a small benefit? I sent before thee Moses, my chosen servant, and instructed him that he might be your leader and lawgiver. I sent with him Aaron, that he might be your priest and transact all spiritual matters between myself and you, in offerings, sacrifices, and atonements. I sent Miriam, to whom I gave the spirit of prophecy, that she might tell you things to come, and be the director of your females. To this sense the Chaldee, "I have sent three prophets before you; Moses, that he might teach you the tradition of judgments, Aaron, that he might make atonement for the people; and Miriam, that she might instruct the females."
entries.15d26a229352f6a85b028a93d5b1732ac872f3c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34854" type="x-p"/> Remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted - He sent for Balaam to curse your fathers; but by my influence he was obliged to bless them. See Numbers 22 (note) and Numbers 23 (note), and the notes there, where this subject is largely considered. <div eID="gen34854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34855" type="x-p"/> From Shittim unto Gilgal - From the encampment at Shittim, <reference osisRef="Num.25.1">Num 25:1</reference>, on the way to that of Gilgal, <reference osisRef="Jos.4.19">Jos 4:19</reference>. Balaam gave different answers in the interval between these places. We may suppose that the encampments of Israel advanced slowly to that part of Jordan which was opposite to Gilgal. The Chaldee has, "Were there not wonderful things done in your behalf from the valley of Shittim to the house of Gilgal?" See <reference osisRef="Jos.3.1">Jos 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jos.4.20">Jos 4:20</reference>. Thus there will be a reference to the miraculous passage over Jordan. See Newcome. <div eID="gen34855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34856" type="x-p"/> That ye may know the righteousness - The just, equitable, and merciful dealing of the Most High. Recollect those things, that ye may have a proper impression of this. There are many interpretations given of this rather obscure clause; what I have proposed seems to me the most simple. <div eID="gen34856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34857" type="x-p"/> This is the sum of the address; and here the case of the plaintiff terminates, the prisoners being called to show why the sentence of the law should not be pronounced. I make no apology for using any forensic terms, as the passages before us refer to a case brought into a court to be judged, and the terms in the original are all such as are proper for a court of justice; and the thing itself is called the Lord's controversy, ריב יהוה rib Yehovah, Jehovah's suit at law. And hence it is said, He will plead, litigate, with Israel.
entries.8a2018172c69246b5a5566366be6076200935a0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34858" type="x-p"/> Wherewith shall I come before the Lord - Now the people, as defendants, appear; but instead of vindicating themselves, or attempting to dispute what has been alleged against them, they seem at once to plead guilty; and now anxiously inquire how they shall appease the wrath of the Judge, how they shall make atonement for the sins already committed. <div eID="gen34858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34859" type="x-p"/> Bow myself before the high God - They wish to pray, and to make supplication to their Judge; but how shall they come before him? They have no right to come into his presence. Some offering must be brought; but of what kind, or of what value? Their sin is unprecedented, and usual methods of access will not avail. They are distracted in their minds, and make a variety of proposals to themselves, some rational, some absurd and impossible, and some even sinful. <div eID="gen34859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34860" type="x-p"/> Shall I come before him with burnt-offerings - This is reasonable, and according to the law; but this will be insufficient.
entries.82f5b2f7fa1f18e2b89089bcd646d605b70d121f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34861" type="x-p"/> Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams - These might be procured, though with difficulty; but conscience says neither will these do. <div eID="gen34861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34862" type="x-p"/> With ten thousands of rivers of oil - This is absurd and impossible; but could even these be procured, could they all make atonement for such guilt, and ingratitude, and rebellion? <div eID="gen34862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34863" type="x-p"/> Shall I give my first-born for my transgression - This was sinful and wicked; but such offerings had been made by the Phoenicians, and their successors the Carthaginians, and this very custom was copied by the corrupt Israelites. See some cases of such offerings, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.27">2Kgs 3:27</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Lev.20.27">Lev 20:27</reference> (note). <div eID="gen34863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34864" type="x-p"/> The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? - This clause is an explanation of the former. Shall I make the first-born, the best and goodliest of my children, חטאת chattath, a Sin-Offering for my soul? And thus the original is used in a multitude of places. <div eID="gen34864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34865" type="x-p"/> When they had put all these questions to their reason and conscience, they found no satisfaction; their distraction is increased, and despair is about to take place, when Jehovah, the plaintiff, in his mercy interposes:
entries.5dd3b5b659d1e94902bed21e01244167714c3d13: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34866" type="x-p"/> He hath showed thee, O Man, what is good - All the modes of expiation which ye have proposed are, in the sight of God, unavailable; they cannot do away the evil, nor purify from the guilt of sin. He himself has shown thee what is good; that which is profitable to thee, and pleasing to himself. And what is that? Answer, Thou art: - <div eID="gen34866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34867" type="x-p"/> I. To do justly; to give to all their due. <div eID="gen34867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34868" type="x-p"/> 1. To God his due; thy heart, thy body, soul, and spirit; thy Wisdom, understanding, judgment. "To love him with all thy heart, soul, mind, and strength, and thy neighbor as thyself." This is God's due and right from every man. <div eID="gen34868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34869" type="x-p"/> 2. Thou art to give thy neighbor his due to do to him as thou wouldst that he should do to thee, never working ill to him. <div eID="gen34869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34870" type="x-p"/> 3. Thou art to give to thyself thy due; not to deprive thy soul of what God has provided for it; to keep thy body in temperance, sobriety, and chastity; avoiding all excesses, both in action and passion. <div eID="gen34870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34871" type="x-p"/> II. Thou art to love mercy; not only to do what justice requires, but also what mercy, kindness, benevolence, and charity require. <div eID="gen34871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34872" type="x-p"/> III. But how art thou to do this? Thou art to walk humbly with thy God; הצנע hatsnea, to humble thyself to walk. This implies to acknowledge thy iniquity, and submit to be saved by his free mercy, as thou hast already found that no kind of offering or sacrifice can avail. Without this humiliation of soul there never was, there never can be, any walking With God; for without his mercy no soul can be saved; and he must be Thy God before thou canst walk with him. Many, when they hear the nature of sin pointed out, and the way of salvation made plain through the blood of the Lamb, have shut their eyes both against sin and the proper sacrifice for it, and parried all exhortation, threatening, etc., with this text: "God requires nothing of us but to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with him." Now I ask any man, Art thou willing to stand or fall by this text? And it would cost me neither much time nor much pains to show that on this ground no soul of man can be saved. Nor does God say that this doing justly, etc., shall merit eternal glory. No. He shows that in this way all men should walk; that this is the duty of Every rational being; but he well knows that no fallen soul can act thus without especial assistance from him, and that it is only the regenerate man, the man who has found redemption through the blood of the cross, and has God for His God, that can thus act and walk. Salvation is of the mere mercy of God alone; for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. <div eID="gen34872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34873" type="x-p"/> The manner of raising attention, says Bp. Newcome, on <reference osisRef="Mic.6.1">Mic 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mic 6:2</reference>, by calling on man to urge his plea in the face of all nature, and on the inanimate creation to hear the expostulation of Jehovah with his people, is truly awakening and magnificent. The wards of Jehovah follow in <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3-Mic.6.5">Mic 6:3-5</reference>. And God's mercies having been set before the people, one of them is introduced in a beautiful dramatic form; asking what his duty is towards so gracious a God, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mic 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mic 6:7</reference>. The answer follows in the words of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mic 6:8</reference>. Some think we have a sort of dialogue between Balak and Balaam, represented to us in the prophetical way. The king of Moab speaks, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mic 6:6</reference>. Balaam replies by another question in the two first hemistichs of <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mic 6:7</reference>. The king of Moab rejoins in the remaining part of the verse; and Balaam replies, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mic 6:8</reference>. Bps. Butler and Lowth favor this. I cannot agree.
entries.136cf7e360ced616dea59b5bae3a7ac95ff28f49: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34874" type="x-p"/> The Lord's voice crieth unto the city - No man is found to hear; but the man of wisdom will hear, תושיה tushiyah; a word frequent in the writings of Solomon and Job, signifying wisdom, wealth, substance, reason, essence, happiness; any thing that is complete; or that which is substantial, in opposition to vanity, emptiness, mere show, unsubstantiality. When God speaks, the man of common sense, who has any knowledge of God or his own soul, will see thy name; but instead of יראה yireh, will see, the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic, with twelve of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., have read יראי yirey, they that Fear. The Vulgate reads: - <div eID="gen34874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34875" type="x-p"/> Et salus erit timentibus nomen tuum. "And thou shalt be salvation to them that fear thy name." <div eID="gen34875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34876" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint - Και σωσει φαβουμενους το ονομα αυτου. <div eID="gen34876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34877" type="x-p"/> And he shall save those who fear his name. - <div eID="gen34877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34878" type="x-p"/> This the Arabic copies. <div eID="gen34878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34879" type="x-p"/> The Targum has, "And the teachers shall fear the name." That is, יהוה Yehovah. <div eID="gen34879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34880" type="x-p"/> The French Bible is very strange: - <div eID="gen34880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34881" type="x-p"/> Car ton nom volt comme il va de tout. "For thy name sees how every thing goes." <div eID="gen34881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34882" type="x-p"/> The word תושיה tushiyah, mentioned above, which occasions all the difficulty, has been read with an ע ain by the Vulgate and Septuagint, as coming from the root ישע yasha, to be saved; and it is very likely that this was the original reading. The two last letters in the word, יה, might have been easily mistaken in the MS. for the letter ע where I may suppose the word stood thus, תושע, shall be saved; and as several MSS. read יראי yirey, they who fear, instead of יראה yireh, he shall see, the whole clause might have been just what it appears in the Vulgate and Septuagint. It is also necessary to remark that the word in dispute has various forms in some MSS., which is a strong presumption against its authenticity. See Kennicott and De Rossi.
entries.96c0730a9d7d770778b6d94439fac375e90e1977: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34883" type="x-p"/> Are there yet the treasures of wickedness - Such as false balances and deceitful weights. See on <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">Hos 12:7</reference> (note). This shows that they were not Doing Justly. They did not give to each his due.
entries.c9a91163186d70b4cf81ab1488fc0b4127fa6889: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34884" type="x-p"/> For the rich men thereof are full of violence - This shows that they did not love mercy. <div eID="gen34884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34885" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants thereof have spoken lies - This shows that they did not humble themselves to walk with God.
entries.ab79a83e0534c26fbd3609774b970d92b3b96905: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34886" type="x-p"/> Will I make thee sick in smiting thee - Perhaps better, "I also am weary with smiting thee, in making thee desolate for thy sins." They were corrected, but to no purpose; they had stroke upon stroke, but were not amended.
